WMU348 Aerial Ungulate  Survey (2015 -16) 
Background 
The last survey conducted for a population estimate was in winter of 2010/11 using the random stratified block 
methodology.  S ince previous surveys were conducted later in  January/February when conditions  were 
favourable, the ability to acquire meaningful age data (antler class) on moose and deer at this time due to antler 
drop is difficult and therefore not reported .  Antlered moose are managed on a limited entry hunt with  an 
archery only S1-O31 season and a general N1 -N30 season, there is no antlerless moose season .  M ule deer 
(antlered and antlerless) are also managed through a limited entry hunt N1 -N30 and a general archery only S1-
O31 season.  White-tailed deer (antlered and antlerless) are managed by a ge neral archery only S1-O31 season 
and a general N1-N30 season; up until 2015 two supplemental antlerless tags could also be acquired, however, 
this has currently been reduced to one tag.  
Survey Method 
The objective of this survey was to establ ish population estimates for moose, white -tailed and mule deer; 
including age and sex classifications where possible .  Transects, 10 km in length and oriented north -south, were 
established spatially throughout the WMU at 2 km intervals within a GIS environment.  Based on previous 
survey ungulate densities, transects were randomly selected until 650  kilometres of survey distance was 
achieved, an additional 113 kilometres of transect were flown to increase the sample size of mule deer 
observed.  The su rvey was then flown using distance sampling methodology  as described in the Distance 
Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol Manual (ESRD, 2014).   
Results 
The survey was completed  from December 14-17, 2015. Total ungulates observed were 27 7 moose, 404 white-
tailed deer, 173  mule deer and 67  elk observed from 164, 152, 38, and 9 independent groups, respectively. Of 
the 276 moose that were successfully classified, 159 were cows, 82 were calves, and 36  were bulls; age clas s 
(antler size) of bu lls were 12 (39%) small, 14 (45%) medium, 5 (16 %) large.  Of the 389  white-tailed deer that 
were successfully classified, 205 were does, 149 were fawns, and 50 were bucks; age class (antler size) of bucks 
were 15 (30%) small, 31 (62 %) medium and 4 (8%) large. Of the 167 mule deer that were successfully classified, 
86 were does, 66 were fawns, and 21 were bucks; age class (antler size) of bucks were 12 (57%) small, 8 (38%) 
medium and 1 (5%) large .  Historical population estimates and species densities are  presented in Tables 1 –  3.  
Additional effort was given to locate specific elk herds but success was  limited by fresh snow, therefore an 
overall low elk count was obtained. Of the 67 elk classified, 35 were cows, 20 were calves, and 12 were bulls; 
age class (antler size) of bulls were 8 spike/forks and 4 legal (3-6 point) bulls.
